o1.biggest_strength: A clear no to the 20% cut, backed by correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, net $1,174) and a plain break-even point of $262,500, roughly four top affiliates.
o1.biggest_mistake: The Partner tier's 40% first-year rate raises cost for the top 20 when the complaint was payouts and lost credit, not the rate. The cost of the 90-day window is left vague ('every 10% adds $63,000') instead of being estimated.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Put real dates and owners on the 30-day plan. Estimate what the 90-day window will actually cost. Reward the top tier with service and speed rather than a higher rate, or show more clearly why the extra rate is worth it.

o2.biggest_strength: Honest, quantified decision-making. It points out that the $210k saving only exists if we cut commission on customers already earned (about $38k otherwise), projects the 90-day window cost from our own numbers, and gives a dated 30-day plan with owners.
o2.biggest_mistake: The window projection rests on assumed 65–75% conversion by day 90 and a margin assumption, which makes it denser than grade-7 reading. The detailed legal disclosure wording runs a little heavy for a one-page rule sheet.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Simplify the 'why not 20%' table into plainer words, tighten the rules page, and show a quick sensitivity check on the day-90 conversion assumption.

reason: Both say no to the cut with the right maths, but the second one tells me the uncomfortable truths: the real saving is $38k, not $210k, and this plan costs more. It costs the window, keeps rates flat across tiers, and hands my partner manager a dated plan with owners.
